body:
Thank you for asking. It's necessary for SSR to pass a resolver context to resolver functions. For SSR, it:

0. Starts from `WithApollo.getInitialProps`
1. Creates a resolver context from `req` and `res`
2. Initializes an apollo client instance with [`SchemaLink`](https://github.com/zeit/next.js/pull/11681/files#diff-52c0088e3df4611902ee3b5f59a4a97dR196) with the resolver context
3. Executes `getDataFromTree`, which leads the apollo client to...
4. Pass the resolver context to [resolver functions as the 3rd argument](https://github.com/zeit/next.js/pull/11681/files#diff-682d12e5f9468d1190b78c5c58a34533R5)

To pass a resolver context to resolver functions, we have to take care of two paths.

1. One for an  HTTP request to the GraphQL server (it's in `pages/api/graphql.ts`)
1. Another for SSR, done by `SchemaLink` that allows us to resolve GraphQL query without calling HTTP request.

The above code covers the case no. 2.

As you know, both paths run on the server-side, so here we have to get off client-side execution.

Without this specific change, babel-loader won't transpile files from the mono repo which resolve outside of the next app directory through the `paths` config.

This is particularly important in the case of the example repository I provided which has the following structure:
```
.
└── packages
    ├── bar
    ├── baz
    │   └── src
    ├── foo
    └── web-app
```
In this example when running `yarn --cwd packages/web-app next build`:
`dir` is the directory where `next.config.js` is, which resolves to `./packages/web-app`.
using this as include, prevents babel-loader from transpiling files in `./packages/bar`,`./packages/foo` and `./packages/baz`. Thus when they are resolved through the `paths` configuration in tsconfig, webpack will try to load them directly without transpilation.

body:
That's a valid concern:

> I'm not entirely sure it's the correct behavior given that other packages in a repo are pretty much outside of the scope of Next.js and suddenly compiling them could be an issue...

## Seems to require explicit opt-in

It is worth noting that by default nothing outside the Next root will be compiled - when you set up your project and start using typescript, the generated `tsconfig.json` does not include a `baseUrl`; so compilation will be limited to the Next folder.

A developer has to make a very explicit change to modify the `baseUrl`.

I'm trying to think why would anyone do this (modify baseUrl Next's `tsconfig`, either directly or through `extends`), if their intent is not to have code outside the Next folder compiled. But I cannot, for now at least, see this happening.

## Some background on mono-repos

I'm probably not the common Next user as I've been using Next nearly exclusively with mono-repos (either `docs` or `site`). And these have been either JS or TS.

You always do the same thing:

- You need to add the aliases to the webpack config where:
  - I always used my own bespoke alias resolver as you also often also need it for eslint and babel
  - then also config `baseUrl/paths`  in `tsconfig.json` to keep VScode happy
- Add `next-transpile-modules` so the other packages get compiled and bundled.

Our aliases would point to the `src` folder of the various packages, because Next would be there way before packages even get built into their own dist and published. Next builds for us are always apps/sites - a deployable rather than published package - you want everything bundled (at least everything in the mono-repo, some `node_modules` may flagged as externals, and loaded via `unpkg.com`) .

For us, we always want other packages bundled in both development and production builds - the whole point was that Next would build and bundle the source of other packages. It is an 'integration hub' if you wish.

Then there could be some extra effort in ensuring that when you build each package, aliases are not in force and one package does not bundle the other.

# What other use case then?

So I think there are two questions to be answered:

- When could a developer explicitly modify `baseUrl` yet not wish for anything under that `baseUrl` be complied?
- How could a developer mistakenly modify `baseUrl`?

For security reasons an absolute URL must unfortunately be specified manually.

* It's possible to grab the hostname from the request object (e.g. `req.host`) but that is supplied by the client and can't be trusted.
* You can infer the URL of the instance but it's impossible to guess the intended canonical URL of an instance and that's important for OAuth integration to work

   e.g. callback URLs at `www.example.com` and `example.com` are not the same as far most OAuth providers are concerned - typically it has to match exactly whatever you have told them the URL of your site is.
